candidate_relations.reason: Cockayne-Touraine type is a specific subtype of dominant dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, characterized by localized blistering, but the clinical presentation of pruritus and lichenification points more specifically to EBP, which is also a form of DDEB but distinct from Cockayne-Touraine.

Porphyria Cutanea Tarda is a metabolic disorder with different clinical and histopathological features (e.g., photosensitivity, blistering, hypertrichosis, iron overload) not described here. The genetic finding of COL7A1 mutation is specific to epidermolysis bullosa.
Lichen Simplex Chronicus describes the lichenified plaques, which are a clinical manifestation of chronic scratching, but not the underlying diagnosis of Epidermolysis Bullosa Pruriginosa.

Dermatitis is a very broad term for skin inflammation. While the patient has erythematous and pruritic lesions, 'dermatitis' lacks the specificity of the underlying blistering disorder and genetic cause.
Genodermatosis is a broad category for genetically determined skin disorders. While EBP is a genodermatosis, this term lacks the specificity of the exact diagnosis.

Dermatitis Herpetiformis is an autoimmune blistering disease associated with celiac disease, with distinct clinical features (e.g., grouped vesicles, gluten sensitivity) and histopathology (e.g., granular IgA deposits) not present in this case. The COL7A1 mutation rules this out.
COL7A1 mutation is the genetic cause of Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa, including EBP, but it is not the clinical diagnosis itself.

Epidermolysis Bullosa Simplex involves blistering within the epidermis (keratinocytes), whereas the histopathology shows dermoepidermal separation, characteristic of Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa (due to COL7A1 mutation).

Hallopeau-Siemens type is a severe, generalized recessive form of Dystrophic Epidermolysis Bullosa, which is inconsistent with the localized, progressive, and less severe presentation described (pruriginosa variant). The genetic finding of a heterozygous missense variant also points away from a typical recessive severe form.
Hyperkeratosis is a histopathological finding or clinical feature (thickening of the stratum corneum) that can be present in lichenified plaques, but it is not the underlying diagnosis.

Lichen Sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory skin condition with distinct clinical features (e.g., white, atrophic plaques, often genital) and histopathology (e.g., homogenization of collagen, inflammatory infiltrate) not described in this case.
Dominant dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa is the broader category under which Epidermolysis Bullosa Pruriginosa falls. The reference diagnosis is more specific.

Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin condition with distinct clinical features (e.g., silvery scales on erythematous plaques, specific distribution) and histopathology (e.g., acanthosis, parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses) not described here. The dermoepidermal separation and COL7A1 mutation rule out psoriasis.

Epidermolysis bullosa dystrophica, inversa, is a specific subtype of DDEB characterized by blistering in flexural areas, which is not the primary presentation described (left shin, pruritic, lichenified).

This candidate is a complete equivalent of the reference diagnosis 'Epidermolysis bullosa pruriginosa (EBP)'. The clinical presentation (pruritic, lichenified papules/plaques, milia, erosions, long duration), histopathology (dermoepidermal separation, milia), and genetic finding (COL7A1 mutation) all strongly support this specific diagnosis.
Pruritic Dermatitis describes symptoms (itchy skin inflammation) but does not capture the underlying genetic blistering disorder (Epidermolysis Bullosa Pruriginosa).
